classifications.label: Strategic driver
classifications.meaning: A reason change may be required.

classifications.label: Constraint
classifications.meaning: A factor limiting the options available.

classifications.label: Workforce issue
classifications.meaning: A skills, recruitment or capability concern.

classifications.label: Assumption
classifications.meaning: A belief that needs validating before anyone relies on it.

evidence.text: The CEO frames this as a capability decision, not a software purchase: success means contract wins, engineering effectiveness and resilience, and stagnation would do more damage than temporary disruption.
AeroTech lost a 2025 work package partly because it could not supply model-based definition (MBD) data.
Several competing tier-2 suppliers are investing in integrated digital engineering environments.
The Board will defer the decision entirely if the recommendation doesn't show that implementation risks are understood.
Belief to test: technology risk is bigger than organisational risk. The CEO thinks most teams get this the wrong way round, because organisational change is harder to quantify.
Programmes above £5M receive enhanced Board scrutiny and compete for funding with other strategic investments.
Lost productivity, implementation support and process redesign usually cost more than licences. The 2023 ERP rollout cut engineering output by about 20% for six months, none of it budgeted.
The draft business case puts about 85% of the budget into licences and hardware, leaving little for training, process redesign and change management.
Belief to test: benefits will appear quickly without operational disruption. The Finance Director treats this claim in any business case with scepticism.
Finance does not automatically prefer the cheapest option: a lower-cost choice that weakens capability or forces a second transition later is a false economy.
Critical manufacturing knowledge sits in unofficial workflows: around 400 NC programs rely on in-house post-processor macros that nobody has documented.
Production can't pause for the migration: Airbus and Rolls-Royce delivery schedules run continuously throughout.
Belief to test: existing workflows can be recreated easily in a new environment. Engineering plans assume so; the Manufacturing Director says much of the capability lives in processes, not tools.
Every migrated NC program must be re-verified on the machine before production use, and that validation effort is routinely underestimated.
Better data continuity between design and manufacturing could remove manual hand-offs that cause rework and scrap. Manufacturing warns that over-cautious governance can slow such improvements.
Stress and fatigue analysis depends on scripted links between CATIA V5 and Abaqus; any platform change breaks them until they are rebuilt and re-validated.
The non-negotiable design capabilities are complex surfacing, large-assembly performance and composite design.
Migration will reduce engineering output on live programmes, and the next Airbus work package is due in the middle of any likely transition.
Belief to test: new software automatically improves productivity. The Chief Design Engineer expects 12–18 months before engineers are faster than they are today.
Eight of the 25 most experienced CATIA engineers could retire within five years, and much of their workflow knowledge is undocumented.
Graduates increasingly arrive trained on newer tools; two candidates declined offers in 2025, citing AeroTech's ageing software.
Belief to test: recruitment challenges can be solved through training alone. HR doubts that training budgets will attract engineers who expect modern tools.
Retraining 220 engineering users would take 6–10 days each plus super-user support, a burden on morale during peak delivery.
Belief to test: engineers will accept change. Several senior engineers privately expect any migration to be scaled back or reversed.
Senior engineers say today's workflows work well. Many valuable templates, macros and part-family tables were built by individuals and exist only on their own machines.
Early-career engineers say today's workflows won't suit future engineers, and see modern, connected tools as the sign of a forward-looking employer.
CATIA V5 is moving to sustaining support: fewer fixes, and compatibility with future Windows releases is not assured.
Some engineering workstations run unsupported operating system builds, kept only to run older V5 add-ins.
Defence-related data from BAE Systems work must stay in UK-controlled environments, which limits cloud-hosted options.
A current platform would simplify lifecycle management, patching and licence administration.
AS9100 and customer quality obligations are unchanged whatever the platform; certification cannot lapse during the transition.
Procedures, training records, configuration controls and audit evidence would all need rewriting, work that engineering plans rarely include. Quality insists governance must be protected.
Migrated models must keep a traceable link to released configurations; losing it would be a major audit finding.
Archived V5 data must stay readable for the 20+ year service life of the parts AeroTech supports.
Airbus is watching suppliers' ability to collaborate across increasingly digital supply chains; in its view, failing to evolve carries more strategic risk than the cost of change.
During a supplier's transformation, customers care more about delivery performance than technology ambition.
Belief to test: customer expectations will stay as they are. Airbus expects supplier digital requirements to change significantly within the decade.
Airbus does not mandate a CAD platform; it judges suppliers on the capability their tools enable.
